clinicalPearls: Anti-Ri (ANNA-2) targets the neuronal RNA-binding proteins NOVA-1 and NOVA-2.
In adults it is most often associated with breast and gynaecological cancer and small cell lung carcinoma.
The hallmark presentation is opsoclonus-myoclonus, frequently combined with cerebellar and brainstem signs.
Distinctive brainstem features include jaw dystonia, jaw-opening dystonia, trismus and laryngospasm, which are relatively specific to anti-Ri.
Gait ataxia, dysarthria and truncal instability are common, and some patients develop parkinsonism or a supranuclear gaze disturbance.
Opsoclonus-myoclonus in an adult should prompt onconeural antibody testing and a search for underlying malignancy.
Some patients stabilise or improve with tumour treatment and immunotherapy, although residual disability is common.
The adult opsoclonus-myoclonus of anti-Ri differs from the paediatric form, which is classically linked to neuroblastoma and other antibodies.
reference.pathophysiology: NOVA-1 and NOVA-2 are neuron-specific RNA-binding proteins that regulate alternative splicing of transcripts governing inhibitory neurotransmission, and they are enriched in the brainstem, cerebellum and spinal motor neurons. Breast, gynaecological or small cell lung tumours that ectopically express these onconeural antigens break immune tolerance and generate the anti-Ri antibody as a diagnostic marker, with antigen-specific T-cell responses implicated in tissue injury. Disease preferentially involves the brainstem, including the saccadic and omnipause circuitry whose disruption is thought to release the involuntary conjugate saccades of opsoclonus, together with the cerebellum and motor pathways. Neuronal loss and inflammatory infiltrates in these regions produce the combination of opsoclonus-myoclonus, ataxia, and the characteristic jaw dystonia and laryngospasm.
additionalDifferentials: Other causes of opsoclonus-myoclonus including parainfectious, toxic-metabolic and other onconeural antibody syndromes
Anti-Yo and anti-Hu paraneoplastic cerebellar or brainstem disease
Brainstem encephalitis of infective or demyelinating origin
Idiopathic or genetic movement disorders including dystonia and parkinsonism
Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease when myoclonus is prominent
additionalInvestigations: Serum and cerebrospinal fluid anti-Ri (ANNA-2) with confirmatory immunohistochemistry and line blot
Mammography, breast MRI and pelvic imaging for breast or gynaecological malignancy
CT of the chest and whole-body FDG-PET for small cell lung carcinoma or occult tumour
MRI of the brain to evaluate brainstem and cerebellar signal change
Cerebrospinal fluid for pleocytosis, raised protein and oligoclonal bands
Video-oculography or clinical documentation of opsoclonus and saccadic intrusions
Tumour markers to support an occult breast or gynaecological primary
redFlags: Disabling opsoclonus-myoclonus impairing vision and mobility
Laryngospasm or severe jaw dystonia compromising the airway or feeding
Occult breast, gynaecological or lung malignancy requiring staging
Brainstem involvement threatening bulbar and respiratory function
reference.prognosis: The outcome is variable; a proportion of patients improve or stabilise with early tumour treatment and immunotherapy, but residual ataxia, myoclonus or brainstem signs are common. Prognosis depends substantially on how promptly the underlying malignancy is identified and treated.
pitfalls: Regarding adult opsoclonus-myoclonus as benign or purely parainfectious and omitting a tumour search
Overlooking jaw dystonia, trismus and laryngospasm as clues to anti-Ri
Assuming a paediatric neuroblastoma association in adult patients
Delaying malignancy screening while awaiting antibody confirmation
references: Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
Consensus diagnostic criteria for paraneoplastic neurological syndromes
management: Pursue tumor-directed therapy and neurologic immunotherapy in parallel, not sequentially, once a high-risk phenotype or antibody is identified
Do not wait for antibody confirmation before starting treatment if suspicion for a paraneoplastic neurologic syndrome is high, once infectious causes are reasonably excluded

Manage the underlying breast, gynaecological, or lung malignancy per its own stage-directed surgery, radiotherapy, and systemic therapy; there is no role for surgery or radiotherapy directed at the neurologic syndrome itself
Offer first-line acute immunotherapy with corticosteroids, intravenous immunoglobulin, or plasma exchange for the neurologic syndrome
For non-responders, consider second-line options including an anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody, azathioprine, mycophenolate mofetil, or cyclophosphamide
Consider an interleukin-6 targeted antibody for autoimmune encephalitis refractory to anti-CD20 therapy, recognizing this is a broader PNS-category option rather than anti-Ri specific
Expect a potentially lesser or slower immunotherapy response than surface-antigen paraneoplastic syndromes, since anti-Ri targets intracellular antigens
Use a GABA-enhancing agent such as clonazepam for symptomatic control of the opsoclonus-myoclonus movement disorder
Maintain airway vigilance and supportive management for jaw dystonia, jaw-opening dystonia, trismus, or laryngospasm associated with anti-Ri disease
Repeat malignancy screening every four to six months for up to two years if initial screening is negative in a high-risk phenotype or antibody-positive patient
Use a paraneoplastic risk scoring framework weighing phenotype risk, antibody risk, and whether a consistent cancer has been found to guide diagnostic confidence and ongoing surveillance

Let ongoing neurologic monitoring of gait, speech, eye movements, and swallow or airway status, along with immunotherapy response, guide escalation between first and second line options via multidisciplinary team input
Refer any adult with opsoclonus-myoclonus for onconeural antibody testing and coordinated malignancy workup, involving neurology or neuro-oncology and the relevant oncology subspecialty
Escalate urgently for disabling opsoclonus-myoclonus affecting vision or mobility, or for airway-threatening features such as laryngospasm or severe jaw dystonia or trismus
